name: Lolegaon
tagline: Canopy walk, cypress forest and a Jhandi Dara sunrise
meta_description: Lolegaon (Kafer) travel guide: heritage forest canopy walk, Jhandi Dara sunrise, homestays and the WBFDC lodge, costs, shared jeeps and how to pair it with Lava.
summary: Lolegaon, also called Kafer, is a hill village at about 1,675 m, 24 km from Lava and about 55 km from Kalimpong. It is known for an old cypress and pine forest with a canopy walk and for sunrise over Kanchenjunga at Jhandi Dara. One night is enough; two is restful.
intro: Lolegaon spreads along a ridge at about 1,675 m on NH717A, the road that runs from the Dooars up through Lava toward Sikkim. Locally it is also known as Kafer. The village is small: a few shops, a school, a monastery, terraced fields of ginger, squash and cardamom, and a growing number of homestays. What sets it apart is the forest beside it, a stand of tall old cypress and pine kept as a heritage forest.

Through that forest runs the canopy walk, a series of suspended footbridges about 180 m long that let you walk at branch height among the trunks. A few kilometres above the village, Jhandi Dara, the 'flag hill' named for its prayer flags, is the sunrise point, with a view north across the valleys to the Kanchenjunga range when the sky is clear.

Lolegaon works well paired with Lava, about an hour away by road through forest, and with Rishyap. Many travellers come for one night on a Lava–Lolegaon–Rishyap circuit; we prefer two, so there is one full quiet day for walking, reading and an unhurried dawn. Prices are modest, but transport is not: there is little shared transport for visitors, so budget for a reserved car.

story.title: A village on the road from the Dooars to Tibet
paras: The road through Lolegaon is now NH717A, which links Bagrakote in the Dooars with Gangtok by way of Lava, Algarah and the Sikkim border. Before roads, the hills here were crossed by footpaths that fed the Kalimpong trade, and villages like Lolegaon grew as farming settlements of Lepcha and Nepali families, clearing terraces for maize, millet and later cardamom and ginger.

The heritage forest beside the village survived because it was protected by the forest department. Its tall trees made it the obvious place for the canopy walk, built to give visitors a way into the forest without trampling it. The bridges have been repaired and rebuilt over the years, and parts close after storms. Use it lightly and treat it as part of a protected forest, not an amusement ride.
story.source: Loleygaon and Algarah articles on Wikipedia (NH717A); West Bengal forest department and local accounts of the heritage forest

did_you_know: Lolegaon is also spelt Loleygaon or Lolaegaon, and many locals call the area Kafer.
The village lies on NH717A, the highway that links Bagrakote in the Dooars with Gangtok via Lava and Algarah.
The canopy walk in Lolegaon's heritage forest is a chain of suspended footbridges about 180 m long among old cypress and pine.
facts: Canopy walk, Jhandi Dara sunrise, homestays

highlights.title: Canopy walk in the heritage forest
highlights.text: Suspended footbridges, about 180 m in all, run between the trunks of old cypress and pine. Go early in the morning, when the forest is quiet and birds are active, and expect it to close in heavy rain or for repairs.

highlights.title: Sunrise at Jhandi Dara
highlights.text: A short drive and a walk above the village, Jhandi Dara is a prayer-flagged hilltop facing north. On clear mornings, mostly October to April, the Kanchenjunga range turns pink, then gold, over the valleys.

highlights.title: Village walks
highlights.text: Paths lead through terraced fields of ginger, squash and cardamom, past a small monastery and the school. Walk with your homestay host and you will learn more in an hour about farming in these hills than from any guidebook.

highlights.title: Forest birding
highlights.text: The heritage forest and the road toward Lava hold laughingthrushes, barbets, minivets, flycatchers and woodpeckers. Dawn, before cars start, is the time; a local guide helps you find mixed flocks.

highlights.title: Quiet evenings
highlights.text: There is nothing to do after dark except eat, talk and look at stars, which is the point. Homestays cook dinner at home, and on clear nights the sky over the ridge is very dark.

how_to_reach.text: A few shared jeeps run between Kalimpong and Lolegaon, mostly leaving Kalimpong in the late morning and Lolegaon early in the morning, about ₹150–250 a seat, indicative for 2026, taking 2.5–3 hours. Timings change; ask at the Kalimpong motor stand the day before. Shared transport from Lava is rare.

A reserved car from Lava takes about an hour for the 24 km and costs about ₹1,500–2,500, indicative for 2026. From Kalimpong it costs about ₹3,000–4,000. From NJP or Bagdogra, expect about 120–125 km, 4.5–5 hours and ₹5,000–6,500 per car. Most visitors combine Lolegaon with Lava and Rishyap in one booking.

The nearest airport is Bagdogra (IXB). The nearest major station is New Jalpaiguri (NJP); Malbazar is a smaller station closer if you come up via Gorubathan and Lava. There is no rail link in the hills.

where_to_stay: Lolegaon has a WBFDC Eco Tourism Centre, the forest development corporation's lodge near the heritage forest, with deluxe, super deluxe and VIP rooms at government tariffs and a canteen. Around the village, a dozen or more small family homestays and cottages offer rooms with meals, many facing north toward the mountains; quality varies, so ask for recent photos and confirm hot water. There are no luxury properties. For heritage comfort, stay in Kalimpong and treat Lolegaon as a long day trip, though you would miss sunrise.
costs: Car to Jhandi Dara and back at dawn
budget_tip: Book Lolegaon as part of a single Lava–Rishyap–Lolegaon car package rather than separate one-way transfers; a combined three-day car usually costs less than three one-way bookings.
tips: Book the Jhandi Dara dawn car the evening before; drivers leave around 4:30–5 am in autumn and winter.
Visit the canopy walk in the morning; it is quieter and may close in afternoon rain.
Carry cash; there is no reliable ATM in Lolegaon and network is patchy.
Ask your homestay for a meal plan; there are few eateries outside the small bazaar.
Bring a torch for the village paths after dark.

experiences.title: Canopy walk in Lolegaon's heritage forest
experiences.summary: Walk at branch height through a stand of old cypress and pine on a chain of suspended footbridges about 180 m long, in the protected heritage forest beside Lolegaon. Short, gentle and best in the quiet of early morning.
body: The heritage forest at Lolegaon is a protected stand of tall, old trees, mostly cypress and pine, on the slope below the village. The canopy walk is a series of suspended footbridges strung between platforms, about 180 m in total, which lets you walk among the trunks well above the forest floor. The bridges sway a little, which children enjoy and nervous adults should know about.

Go early. From about 8 am the forest is still, light comes through in shafts, and birds move through the canopy. By late morning on weekends, groups of day-trippers arrive and it gets noisy. The walk itself takes 20–30 minutes; the forest paths around it add another half hour or so.

The forest department collects a small entry fee at the gate. The walk closes in heavy rain and for maintenance, and parts are sometimes shut for repairs, so check at the gate. Wear shoes with grip, keep to one or two people per bridge section as signposted, and do not lean over the side. It is not suitable for people with a strong fear of heights.

faqs.q: Is the Lolegaon canopy walk open now
faqs.a: It is usually open in daylight hours from autumn to spring, but sections close after storms, in heavy rain and for repairs, sometimes for weeks. Ask your homestay or the WBFDC lodge the evening before, or check at the forest gate. Check current status before you travel if the canopy walk is the main reason for your trip.

faqs.q: Is the Lolegaon canopy walk safe for children
faqs.a: Generally yes for children who can walk steadily and hold the rope rails. The bridges sway and are a few metres above the ground, so keep small children close and limit numbers on each section as signposted. Do not run or jump on the bridges. Children with a fear of heights may prefer the forest paths below.

faqs.q: How long is the canopy walk at Lolegaon
faqs.a: The suspended bridges add up to about 180 m, which takes 20–30 minutes at a relaxed pace. With the forest paths and photographs, allow about an hour to an hour and a half. It is a short, gentle outing rather than a trek, and fits easily into a morning before you drive on to Lava or Rishyap.

experiences.title: Kanchenjunga sunrise at Jhandi Dara
experiences.summary: Drive up before dawn to Jhandi Dara, the prayer-flagged hilltop above Lolegaon, and watch the Kanchenjunga range catch first light across the valleys. Cold, early and, on a clear morning, the best moment of a Lolegaon stay.
body: Jhandi Dara means 'flag hill', after the prayer flags that crowd its top. It lies a few kilometres above Lolegaon, reached by car and a short walk. From the top you look north across forested ridges and deep valleys to the Kanchenjunga range, which at 8,586 m is the third-highest mountain in the world.

Leave around 4:30–5 am in autumn and winter, a little earlier in spring, so you are in place before the first light touches the summit. On a clear morning the peaks go from grey to pink to gold in about twenty minutes. Clouds can roll in quickly, so do not linger over coffee before leaving. Carry a flask of tea, a warm jacket, gloves and a torch.

Clear dawns are most likely from October to December and on many mornings from January to April. In May and the monsoon months, mist usually hides the range. Book the car with your homestay the evening before; drivers know the way in the dark and the best place to stand.

faqs.q: How far is Jhandi Dara from Lolegaon
faqs.a: Jhandi Dara is a few kilometres above Lolegaon, roughly 15–20 minutes by car plus a short walk to the top. Most visitors go by reserved car at dawn, costing about ₹500–900 return, indicative for 2026, arranged through their homestay or lodge. Fit walkers can hike up in about an hour, with a torch.

faqs.q: What is the best month for the Jhandi Dara sunrise
faqs.a: October to December gives the clearest dawns, with November usually the most reliable. January to April also has many clear mornings, though spring haze can soften the view. From May to September, clouds and mist usually block the mountains. Whatever the month, a clear evening is a good sign for the next dawn.

faqs.q: What should I carry to Jhandi Dara
faqs.a: Carry a warm jacket, hat and gloves, as dawn is cold for most of the year, plus a torch for the path, a flask of tea and a camera with a spare battery, since cold drains batteries. Wear shoes with grip. There are no shops at the top, and toilets are not available.

experiences.title: Village and farm walk around Lolegaon
experiences.cost: Free with your homestay host; tip ₹200–500, indicative
experiences.summary: Walk the terraces and lanes of Lolegaon with your homestay host, past ginger, squash and cardamom fields, a small monastery and the village school, and learn how families here farm, cook and make a living in the hills.
body: Lolegaon is a farming village before it is a tourist stop. Terraces below the road grow maize, ginger, potatoes and greens, and many families keep cows and goats. Squash vines, called iskus locally, climb over fences and roofs and appear on almost every dinner table. Lower and wetter slopes hold black cardamom under shade trees.

Ask your homestay host to walk you around for an hour or two in the morning. You will pass houses with drying racks of maize, a small monastery with prayer flags, the school and the little bazaar on the highway. Hosts usually explain what grows when, how the monsoon shapes the year and how homestays have changed village income.

Walk on paths, not through fields, and ask before photographing people or entering any building. A tip for your guide-host is welcome; ₹200–500 is fair for a two-hour walk, indicative for 2026. If you buy ginger, cardamom or local pickles, buy directly from families rather than from roadside middlemen.

faqs.q: What crops grow around Lolegaon
faqs.a: Families around Lolegaon grow maize, ginger, potatoes, squash and leafy greens on terraces, with black cardamom in shaded, wetter areas. Kalimpong district and Sikkim together produce a large share of India's ginger. Many households also keep cows for milk and churpi. Crops vary with altitude, so ask your host what is in season during your visit.

faqs.q: Is there a monastery in Lolegaon
faqs.a: Yes, a small village monastery with prayer flags serves the Buddhist families of Lolegaon. It is a community place of worship rather than a large tourist site. Visitors can usually look in quietly; remove shoes if asked, walk clockwise, and do not photograph inside without permission. Your homestay host can introduce you.

faqs.q: Can I buy local produce in Lolegaon
faqs.a: Yes. Homestay families often sell ginger, cardamom, pickles, honey and churpi, and the small bazaar has seasonal produce. Prices are usually fair. Buying directly from families keeps more money in the village. Pack spices and pickles well for the drive, and check airline rules if flying with liquids.

experiences.title: Homestay kitchen dinner in Lolegaon
experiences.cost: Usually included in homestay meal plans
experiences.summary: Spend an evening in a Lolegaon homestay kitchen as dinner is cooked over the stove: squash curry, dal, rice, greens, gundruk soup, pickles and, if you ask ahead, local chicken or sel roti. Simple, seasonal food that tells you about the hills.
body: Most homestays in Lolegaon cook dinner for their guests, and the kitchen is the warmest room in the house. Ask if you can sit in while the food is made. A typical meal is rice, dal, a squash or potato curry, sautéed greens such as rayo saag, a fresh tomato or chilli pickle, and often a chicken or egg curry for those who want it.

Look out for gundruk, fermented and dried leafy greens made after the harvest and cooked into a sour soup, and kinema, fermented soybeans, both old Nepali hill foods. Breakfast may bring sel roti, a ring-shaped fried rice bread, or puri and potato. Hosts adjust spice levels happily if you ask.

Tell your host in the afternoon if you have dietary needs or want something special, as ingredients come from the village and the small bazaar. Meals are usually included in the room price. Help clear plates, thank the cook, and ask for recipes; many hosts are pleased to share.

faqs.q: What food is served in Lolegaon homestays
faqs.a: Expect home-style Nepali and Indian food: rice, dal, squash or potato curry, greens, pickles and usually chicken or egg curry, with roti on request. Breakfast is often puri, potato curry, eggs or sel roti. Some hosts cook gundruk soup or kinema. Vegetarian meals are easy to arrange; tell your host in advance.

faqs.q: Are meals included in Lolegaon homestay rates
faqs.a: Most homestays quote a per-person rate that includes dinner and breakfast, and sometimes lunch, at roughly ₹1,200–2,200 per person a night, indicative for 2026. Confirm what is included when booking, and whether bottled water, tea through the day and special dishes cost extra. Few eateries are open in the evening.

faqs.q: Can homestays in Lolegaon make Bengali or Jain food
faqs.a: Many hosts are used to guests from Kolkata and can make simple Bengali-style fish or vegetable dishes if ingredients are available, though fish is not always on hand in the hills. Jain or no-onion, no-garlic meals are possible with notice. Mention dietary needs at booking and confirm again on arrival.

faqs.q: Is Lolegaon worth visiting
faqs.a: Yes, for a quiet night or two in a forest village with a good chance of a Kanchenjunga sunrise. The canopy walk, Jhandi Dara and village walks fill a relaxed day. It is not a sightseeing hub, and there is little to do after dark. Pair it with Lava and Rishyap for a three- or four-night village circuit.

faqs.q: How far is Lolegaon from Kalimpong and Lava
faqs.a: Lolegaon is about 24 km from Lava, roughly an hour by car, and about 55 km from Kalimpong, around 2.5–3 hours depending on the route. From Siliguri it is about 120–125 km. Shared jeeps are few, so most visitors use a reserved car, especially when combining it with Lava and Rishyap.

faqs.q: Which is better, Lolegaon or Rishyap
faqs.a: Rishyap, at about 2,590 m, has the wider and closer Kanchenjunga panorama and is colder. Lolegaon, at about 1,675 m, is milder and has the heritage forest with the canopy walk and the Jhandi Dara sunrise. If you have time, do both; they are about 1.5–2 hours apart by road via Lava.

faqs.q: Is one night enough in Lolegaon
faqs.a: One night covers the canopy walk, an evening in the village and the Jhandi Dara sunrise, if the weather allows. Two nights give you a spare dawn in case the first is cloudy, and a full day to walk and rest. We usually suggest two nights between October and December, when views are best.

faqs.q: Can I see Kanchenjunga from Lolegaon
faqs.a: Yes, from Jhandi Dara above the village and from some homestays on the ridge, on clear mornings. The best months are October to December, with many clear mornings from January to April. From May to September, clouds usually hide the range. Sunrise is the best time.

faqs.q: How do I book the WBFDC lodge at Lolegaon
faqs.a: Book through the West Bengal Forest Development Corporation website, wbfdc.net, which opens bookings about three months ahead. The lodge's official postal address is Gitdabling, the post office that serves Lolegaon. Rooms are simple, with a canteen. Weekend dates in spring and October go first, so book early.

faqs.q: Is there an ATM and network in Lolegaon
faqs.a: Do not rely on an ATM in Lolegaon; withdraw cash in Kalimpong or Siliguri. Mobile coverage is patchy and varies by network and by house; data may work only in certain spots. Some homestays have Wi-Fi, often slow. UPI payments work when the network does, so carry enough cash as backup.

faqs.q: Is Lolegaon good for families with children
faqs.a: Yes. Children usually enjoy the canopy walk, the forest and village animals, and homestays are welcoming. Pack warm clothes, snacks and basic medicines, as shops are few and the nearest hospital is in Kalimpong. Keep small children close on the canopy bridges, which sway and are raised above the ground.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Lolegaon
faqs.a: October to December is best for clear mountain views and dry weather, and March to May for flowers, birds and mild temperatures. January and February are clear but cold at night. Avoid mid-June to mid-September, when heavy rain, leeches and landslides on the access roads make travel difficult.
